request_text:
Understood. Here is the revised standalone plan with the migration section removed.

1. Objective

Autoloop should support Claude by invoking the user’s locally installed claude CLI in headless print mode, not by embedding the Agent SDK. That matches Anthropic’s documented scripted interface (claude -p), gives autoloop a stable machine-readable result format (--output-format json with result and session_id), and avoids the SDK path that Anthropic explicitly says is not permitted for consumer OAuth credentials outside Claude Code / Claude.ai.

The target is “as close as possible” parity with the current Codex CLI path, while preserving the user’s existing Claude Code environment. In practical terms, that means durable sessions, resumable runs, provider-neutral orchestration, canonical loop-control output, and minimal interference with Claude’s own configured settings, memory, hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, and output style.

2. Core design decisions

Autoloop will treat Claude as a CLI provider, not an SDK provider. The only supported integration path is spawning the claude binary as a subprocess, passing a prompt, and parsing structured output. Anthropic documents claude -p, --output-format json, and --resume as the supported headless/session mechanisms, and claude auth status as the standard way to verify local authentication.

Autoloop will not use --bare by default. --bare deliberately skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md, which is the opposite of the requirement to leverage the user’s existing Claude Code setup. Claude’s settings docs also make clear that command-line arguments sit above local, project, and user settings in precedence, so the correct way to preserve the user’s configuration is to avoid unnecessary override flags.

Autoloop should therefore use normal claude -p mode and append its orchestration prompt rather than replacing Claude’s system prompt. Anthropic explicitly recommends the append prompt flags for most use cases because they preserve Claude Code’s built-in capabilities while adding custom requirements.

3. Provider abstraction changes inside autoloop

Before adding Claude-specific process calls, autoloop should extract a provider-neutral interface from the current Codex path. The provider contract should accept prompt text, working directory, optional model override, optional effort override, a persisted provider session identifier, and provider-specific automation options. It should return final assistant text, provider session identifier, raw provider payload, and categorized execution status.

Persisted run/session state should be generalized from the current Codex-oriented thread_id concept to a provider-neutral session_id, and each saved session should also record provider. Resuming a saved run with a different provider should fail fast unless the user explicitly starts a new provider session.

Backward compatibility matters here. Existing Codex runs should keep working unchanged. For old saved state, autoloop should load legacy thread_id into the new neutral session field and infer provider="codex" when no provider is recorded.

4. Claude command strategy

The default fresh-turn Claude invocation should be:

claude -p "$PROMPT" \
  --output-format json \
  --append-system-prompt-file "$AUTOLOOP_PROMPT_FILE"

The default resumed-turn invocation should be:

claude -p "$PROMPT" \
  --output-format json \
  --append-system-prompt-file "$AUTOLOOP_PROMPT_FILE" \
  --resume "$SESSION_ID"

This command shape uses only documented headless CLI features: print mode, structured JSON output, appended system-prompt files, and explicit session resume. --resume is the correct primitive for continuing a specific Claude session, and --output-format json gives a stable payload containing the final text result, session ID, and metadata.

Autoloop should not pass --system-prompt or --system-prompt-file in the default Claude mode, because those replace Claude’s default system prompt. The whole point of this integration is to inherit the user’s existing Claude environment and built-in coding behavior while layering autoloop’s phase instructions on top. Anthropic’s docs explicitly say append flags preserve Claude Code’s built-in capabilities and replacement flags are for complete system-prompt control.

Autoloop should also not pass --bare, --setting-sources, --strict-mcp-config, --tools, --disallowedTools, or --disable-slash-commands by default. Those flags are all real Claude CLI features, but each one suppresses or narrows part of the user’s configured environment. Since command-line flags outrank local/project/user settings, using them by default would undermine the requirement to leverage existing Claude setup.

5. What “existing Claude setup” means in practice

Autoloop’s default Claude mode should intentionally inherit all of the following, because Claude Code documents them as part of normal session startup and project configuration: user/project/local settings, CLAUDE.md, auto memory, output style, hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, and built-in or custom subagents.

That inheritance is not just conceptual. Claude’s docs say CLAUDE.md and auto memory are loaded at the start of every conversation, output style instructions are added to the system prompt at session start, hooks are user-defined commands that execute automatically at lifecycle points, skills are automatically added to Claude’s toolkit, plugin components can include hooks, skills, MCP, LSP, and agents, and built-in subagents such as Explore and Plan can be invoked automatically.

Because autoloop is deliberately inheriting this environment, the integration must treat configuration-driven behavior as part of the supported contract, not as accidental noise. That means compatibility testing has to cover repos with CLAUDE.md, local output styles, hooks, skills, plugins, MCP, and subagents enabled.

6. Prompt contract and loop-control rules

Autoloop must keep its existing producer/verifier protocol and continue to treat the canonical loop-control block as the authoritative handoff between the agent and the orchestrator. Claude-specific support should not invent a second clarification system, second approval channel, or second completion contract.

This matters because Claude’s built-in tool universe includes tools that can bypass autoloop’s orchestration model. Anthropic documents tools such as AskUserQuestion, Agent, EnterPlanMode, ExitPlanMode, EnterWorktree, Skill, WebFetch, WebSearch, MCP resource tools, task-management tools, and standard file/bash tools like Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep, and Bash.

Because default Claude mode is intentionally not restricting tools, the appended autoloop prompt must explicitly tell Claude to keep clarifications and completion decisions inside autoloop’s loop-control format, rather than using out-of-band question tools or plan/worktree/task features. In other words, preserve Claude’s environment, but make autoloop’s orchestration contract the top-level behavioral rule for these runs.

The plan should also include a fallback if real-world testing shows that unrestricted Claude environments regularly violate the loop-control contract. That fallback should be an opt-in strict mode, not the default. Strict mode can later add --disable-slash-commands, --tools, or --disallowedTools to narrow behavior when a user wants more determinism than default Claude mode provides. Those flags are documented and available, but they should remain off in the default path.

7. Session lifecycle and persistence

Autoloop’s Claude adapter should parse the JSON result as its canonical payload. Anthropic documents that --output-format json returns structured JSON containing the text result in result, plus session ID and metadata. That final JSON object is the correct source of truth for phase output, session persistence, and post-run bookkeeping.

On every successful Claude turn, autoloop should persist provider="claude", session_id, any explicit model override, any explicit effort override, and raw provider metadata for diagnostics.

On resume, autoloop should call claude -p ... --resume "$SESSION_ID" and continue the same Claude conversation. It should refuse to resume a Claude run through the Codex provider or vice versa.

Autoloop should also keep its own max_iterations semantics separate from Claude’s --max-turns. Anthropic documents --max-turns as the cap on agentic turns inside one print-mode invocation, not an outer workflow loop count. So autoloop should leave --max-turns unset in the default Claude provider and continue to use its own producer/verifier loop counting independently.

For richer telemetry later, autoloop can add an optional stream-json mode, because Anthropic documents --output-format stream-json together with --verbose and --include-partial-messages. But that should be a phase-two enhancement. The first working Claude provider should use plain JSON output for simplicity and stability.

8. Model and effort behavior

To preserve the user’s existing Claude configuration, autoloop should not pass --model or --effort by default. Claude’s settings and CLI docs show that users can configure model behavior persistently, that model aliases such as sonnet and opus are available, that runtime defaults depend on account and configuration, and that --effort is a session-scoped override. That means the right default is to let the user’s Claude setup decide unless autoloop has been explicitly configured to override it.

When autoloop does expose Claude-specific overrides, they should be optional and explicit. A reasonable provider config shape is:

provider:
  name: claude
  claude:
    model: null
    effort: null
    permission_strategy: inherit

inherit should mean: do not pass --model, --effort, or permission flags unless explicitly configured.

9. Permission strategy

Because the default requirement is to leverage existing Claude setup, autoloop’s default permission strategy should be inherit. That means no --permission-mode, no --allowedTools, and no --dangerously-skip-permissions. Claude’s permission behavior will then follow the user’s configured rules and modes. Claude’s docs describe allow/ask/deny permission rules, note that rules come from settings, and document permission modes such as default, acceptEdits, plan, dontAsk, and bypassPermissions.

Autoloop should still support optional permission strategies for users who want more Codex-like automation:
	•	inherit: default, preserve existing Claude behavior
	•	allow_core_tools: pass --allowedTools "Read,Write,Edit,Glob,Grep,Bash" to reduce prompts for the standard file/search/bash toolset
	•	bypass: pass --dangerously-skip-permissions for isolated environments only

Anthropic documents that --allowedTools makes matching tools run without prompts and that --tools is the flag for restricting tool availability. Anthropic also warns that bypass mode still prompts for writes to .git, .claude, .vscode, and .idea, and should be used only in isolated environments such as containers or VMs.

Autoloop should not use --permission-prompt-tool in the first Claude release. Anthropic documents that feature for non-interactive permission handling, but it would introduce another external dependency and another control surface. The v1 behavior should be simpler: if the chosen permission strategy leads to a permission failure, autoloop logs the raw Claude output and exits with a clear message telling the user to adjust Claude permissions or choose a different autoloop permission strategy.

10. Preflight and failure handling

The Claude provider should perform a clear preflight before the first phase turn:
	1.	verify the binary with claude --version
	2.	verify local authentication with claude auth status
	3.	fail early with a provider-specific setup error if either check fails

Anthropic’s CLI reference documents claude auth status as JSON-producing and returning exit code 0 when logged in and 1 when not. Their troubleshooting/setup guidance also recommends verifying the binary directly when diagnosing install/startup issues.

All Claude subprocess calls should be executed without a shell, using a list-of-args subprocess API, and all stdout/stderr should be captured into autoloop’s existing raw logs. If Claude exits non-zero or returns malformed JSON, autoloop should preserve the raw provider payload for debugging and treat the phase as a provider failure, not a loop-control parse failure.

11. Configuration

The provider config should become explicit and nested, so Codex and Claude can coexist cleanly. A practical structure is:

provider:
  name: codex | claude
  codex:
    model: gpt-5.4
    model_effort: null
  claude:
    model: null
    effort: null
    permission_strategy: inherit
runtime:
  pairs: plan,implement,test
  max_iterations: 15
  phase_mode: single
  intent_mode: preserve
  full_auto_answers: false
  no_git: false

That design keeps current Codex behavior stable while giving Claude its own optional knobs.

12. Test plan

The Claude provider should be validated in three layers.

First, provider-agnostic unit tests:
	•	provider selection and config parsing
	•	session-state migration from legacy thread_id to neutral session_id
	•	refusal to resume a run with a different provider
	•	unchanged Codex behavior after the provider abstraction refactor

Second, Claude adapter unit tests with mocked subprocess output:
	•	fresh-turn command construction
	•	resumed-turn command construction with --resume
	•	omission of --bare in default mode
	•	omission of model/effort flags when unset
	•	JSON parsing of result and session_id
	•	error handling for non-zero exit and malformed JSON
	•	permission-strategy flag mapping

Third, live integration tests against a real local Claude install:
	•	new session via claude -p --output-format json
	•	resumed session via --resume
	•	plan/implement/test runs in default inherit permission mode
	•	optional allow_core_tools mode
	•	optional bypass mode in an isolated environment
	•	runs in repos with CLAUDE.md
	•	runs with custom output styles
	•	runs with hooks configured
	•	runs with skills, plugins, MCP servers, and subagents present
	•	validation that canonical autoloop loop-control output still drives the orchestration loop under representative Claude setups

Those live tests are necessary because Claude’s documented configuration surface is broad: CLAUDE.md, auto memory, output styles, hooks, skills, plugins, MCP, and subagents can all affect session behavior.

A particularly important live test is config drift across sessions. Claude’s docs say output style is added to the system prompt at session start and changes take effect the next time you start a new session; CLAUDE.md and auto memory are also loaded at the start of every conversation. That means autoloop must explicitly test what happens when a user changes Claude configuration between an initial run and a resumed run.

13. Rollout plan

Roll this out in four stages.

Stage 1: extract the provider abstraction and move current Codex behavior behind it with no behavior change.

Stage 2: add the Claude CLI adapter behind provider.name = claude, using the default command strategy described above.

Stage 3: run live validation in representative repos that actually use Claude Code configuration features.

Stage 4: add optional strict-mode and stronger automation knobs only if real testing shows the default inherited Claude environment is too nondeterministic for some teams.

That rollout order keeps the risky parts isolated and preserves a clean rollback path.

14. Definition of done

This feature is done when all of the following are true:
	•	autoloop can start a Claude-backed session with claude -p
	•	autoloop can resume the same Claude conversation with stored session_id
	•	autoloop parses Claude JSON output reliably and persists the right metadata
	•	default Claude mode leverages the user’s existing Claude Code setup instead of bypassing it
	•	optional explicit model/effort/permission overrides work when requested
	•	canonical autoloop loop-control behavior still governs plan/implement/test orchestration
	•	Codex behavior remains unchanged
	•	no Anthropic/Claude SDK is used anywhere in the implementation

That is the revised standalone plan with the migration section removed.
